name: Salamina
title: Salamina Ship Thickness Gauging | Ampelakia Docks & Anchorage
description: Thickness gauging at Salamina for tankers, bulk carriers, coasters and tugs at the Ampelakia floating docks, Kynosoura quays and anchorages: hull and tank UTM.
h1: Hull and Tank Thickness Measurement for Ships at Salamina Island
intro: Salamina lies across a narrow strait from Perama, and its eastern shore has become a ship-repair coast in its own right: floating docks at Ampelakia, afloat repair and recycling at Kynosoura, and sheltered water where idle ships wait. Tankers, bulk carriers, coasters, tugs and island ferries come here for docking, repairs and lay-up, which keeps them still long enough for proper gauging. Each job is staffed by technicians who fly in from India and join the vessel wherever it lies.

highlights.p: The Spanopoulos yard at Ampelakia runs floating docks of different sizes beside its quays, lifting workboats and coasters as well as larger merchant hulls. Bottom shell, sea chests and the stern area can be measured while the ship sits dry, with renewal agreed before she refloats.

highlights.h: Afloat repair and recycling at Kynosoura
highlights.p: Kynosoura Dockyard, on the island's eastern point, repairs ships afloat along its main pier and on slipways and also recycles them. Ships going into repair gain from early readings, while ships heading for demolition need their hazardous-materials paperwork in order more than a hull survey.

The bays around Ampelakia and along the eastern coast shelter ships waiting for repair slots, buyers or employment. Such stays run for weeks, so tanks can be opened one after another and a full condition picture built without a docking deadline pressing on the crew.

port.h: Salamina: the island side of the Saronic repair zone
p: Salamina is the large island that closes off the Bay of Elefsina from the Saronic Gulf, separated from Perama on the mainland by a strait that takes only minutes to cross. Car ferries shuttle between Paloukia and Perama throughout the day, which makes the island easy to reach and part of the same working waterfront. The eastern shore, around Ampelakia and the Kynosoura peninsula, faces the Perama repair zone directly, and its bays are deep and protected enough for merchant ships to lie at anchor or alongside. The Hellenic Navy's main base also occupies part of this coast, so movements in some nearby waters are restricted, and the ship's agent and the local harbour master decide where a merchant vessel may lie while it waits or works.

Unlike Piraeus, Salamina has little cargo trade of its own. Ships arrive for what can be done to them rather than for what they carry: dockings and repairs, conversions, retrofits, lay-up and, at the end of a career, recycling. The mix is wide. Product and chemical tankers, small and mid-size bulk carriers and general cargo ships come for repair; tugs, workboats, barges and bunker tankers from the Piraeus harbour fleet use the island's yards for routine docking; domestic ferries and day-cruise vessels winter here between seasons; and yachts and fishing vessels fill the smaller slipways along the coast. Many of the owners using Salamina are the same Athens and Piraeus managers who use Perama, and they choose the island when its docks or quays fit the ship and the dates better.

The waters off Ampelakia and between Salamina and the mainland are among the most sheltered in Attica, which is why ships have long been laid up here when markets turned weak or a sale dragged on. Weather rarely stops a launch transfer for long, although strong northerlies in summer and southerly gales in winter can make boarding at the more open anchorages uncomfortable. There is no tide worth planning around. What really shapes the work is the yard calendar: winter is the busy season for ferry and harbour-craft dockings, while merchant ship repairs follow survey dates and the charter market through the year. Gauging requested at short notice is easiest on a ship already lying idle in a bay; inside a yard, the slot has to be fitted around the docking plan.

facilities.h: Where ships are gauged on and around Salamina
p: The Spanopoulos yard at Ampelakia covers both ends of the market. Its floating docks lift workboats, tugs, coasters and larger merchant ships, and its quays take vessels for afloat work. When a merchant ship is lifted, the dock period is the time to measure bottom and bilge plating, sea chests, the rudder and the stern frame, and to confirm suspect side shell before the yard closes up. On the smaller craft that make up much of the island's repair work, a docking survey tends to find wastage around sea chests, at the boundaries of fuel and ballast tanks and in the shell near the waterline, so short, focused gauging scopes are common and are usually booked once the lift date is fixed.

Kynosoura Dockyard on the eastern side of the island repairs ships afloat along its main pier and builds smaller vessels on its slipways, while its recycling activity brings end-of-life tonnage to the same shoreline. For ships in repair there, gauging is fitted around the steel and pipe renewal already under way. For idle ships in the bays, the agent arranges launches and the crew prepares tanks over several days. Because the Perama quays are a short boat ride away, one mobilisation can cover a ship on each side of the strait. Ships too large for the island's docks are taken to the bigger yards on the mainland side of the bay instead.
list: Spanopoulos shipyard, Ampelakia: floating-dock gauging of bottom shell, sea chests, rudder and stern frame on merchant ships, tugs and coasters
Ampelakia repair quays: afloat repair periods, with deck, tank and piping readings taken alongside the steel and pipe work
Kynosoura Dockyard main pier: gauging during afloat repairs, ballast water system retrofits and coating work on tankers and bulk carriers
Slipways and smaller yards along the eastern shore: shell and tank gauging on harbour craft, ferries, fishing vessels and workboats
Sheltered anchorages and lay-up berths off Ampelakia: condition, pre-sale and reactivation gauging by launch over several days

context.h: Port control, harbour craft and end-of-life ships at Salamina
p: Salamina comes under the Paris MoU, and port state control and harbour supervision are carried out by the Hellenic Coast Guard, through the island's own harbour master and the wider Piraeus organisation. Foreign-flagged ships lying here for repair or lay-up remain liable to inspection, and a ship reactivating after a long idle period is a natural candidate, because PSC officers know what months of standing still do to fire mains, ballast piping and lifesaving appliances. Every ship calling at an EU port must also hold an Inventory of Hazardous Materials under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation, a requirement that weighs more heavily at Salamina than at most ports, given the recycling activity on the island.

The harbour fleet gives Salamina a second inspection market. Tugs, bunker barges, small tankers and passenger vessels working the Piraeus area are surveyed under Greek flag rules or by their class, and their owners dock them on the island regularly. Their steel ages in particular ways: bunker tankers in their cargo and ballast tank boundaries, tugs in the fendering zones and around the towing gear, passenger craft in vehicle decks and voids. Gauging on these vessels is usually done in dock, at short notice, with a scope set by the attending surveyor. For the larger merchant ships repaired here, the logic is the same as across the strait: readings taken before or at the start of a repair let the yard order plate and plan its labour.

jobs.h: Gauging jobs that come up at Salamina
jobs.p: Salamina jobs follow the island's role as a place to dock, repair and wait. Some are short dock-period scopes on harbour craft and coasters, booked a few days ahead once the yard confirms the lift. Others run longer on merchant ships in repair or lying idle, where the superintendent wants a full set of readings before choosing what to renew, where to dock next or whether to sell. A few are tied to end-of-life decisions. We agree with the superintendent which spaces matter most, how the crew or yard will make them safe, and how results are passed back while the ship is still at the island. Typical requests include:
list: Docking-survey gauging of a Piraeus bunker tanker on a floating dock at Ampelakia: bottom and side shell, cargo tank boundaries and sea chests.
Condition gauging of a Handysize bulk carrier lying idle off Ampelakia, so the owner can choose between reactivation and sale with measured hold and ballast tank data.
Pre-docking readings on a product tanker during an afloat repair at Kynosoura, ahead of its intermediate survey.
Winter-refit gauging of a domestic ro-pax ferry's car deck, voids and ballast tanks before the island timetable restarts.
Shell gauging on a harbour tug during its routine docking, with dye penetrant checks on the welds of the towing hook foundation.
Scrubber overboard piping thickness checks on a bulk carrier waiting in the bay for a repair slot.

logistics: The team lands at Athens International Airport and travels by road to Perama, crossing to Salamina on the car ferry to Paloukia, or reaching ships at anchor by launch from the mainland side. Yard entry at Ampelakia or Kynosoura and launch bookings for vessels in the bay are made through the ship's agent, who receives crew details and technician certificates in advance. Technicians need Schengen visas issued in India, so we start applications as soon as the docking or lay-up dates are known and keep the agent updated on travel.

faqs.q: Can a ship laid up off Ampelakia be gauged without moving it?
faqs.a: Yes. Ships lying idle in Salamina's sheltered bays are reached by launch, and the gauging is done where the ship lies. The limiting factor is safe entry: after weeks or months closed, tanks and void spaces must be ventilated, tested and certified by the ship before anyone goes in. With only a skeleton crew aboard, we agree a sequence that suits their capacity, usually starting with ballast tanks and deck.

faqs.q: Do you work inside the Salamina yards, or only for owners?
faqs.a: We work for the owner, manager or buyer of the ship, not as a yard subcontractor. Inside the Spanopoulos yard or at Kynosoura, that means coordinating access, staging, lighting and gas-freeing with the yard through the superintendent, and fitting our sequence around the repair programme. Readings that show substantial or excessive corrosion are marked on the steel and passed to the superintendent and the attending surveyor as each area is finished.

faqs.q: Is a harbour tug or bunker tanker docking worth a mobilisation from India?
faqs.a: On its own, a short docking-survey scope can be a small job for a team travelling from India. Owners of harbour fleets therefore tend to group the work: several craft docking in the same weeks, or one docking combined with a merchant ship under repair at Perama or Kynosoura. Send us the dock dates for all the vessels you have in mind and we plan one trip around them.

faqs.q: What does gauging look like on a ship that is about to be recycled?
faqs.a: Usually there is no thickness survey at all, because the hull's remaining life is no longer the question. What matters for an end-of-life ship calling at an EU port is the Inventory of Hazardous Materials and the documents the recycling facility needs. Gauging becomes relevant only if the owner is still weighing recycling against a further period of trading, when measured hull data can settle the decision.

faqs.q: Can one trip cover ships on both sides of the Salamina strait?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. The Perama repair quays and floating docks are a short boat or ferry crossing from the island, and the Elefsina bay is close by road. If you have one ship docking at Ampelakia and another under repair at Perama, send both programmes and we will plan the order of work and a visa period that covers them, with some margin for slipping dock dates.
